name: Geman Deng
world_status: accessible description is silent on stress

new_statements.quote: The Kman tone system has three phonetic tone heights marked as follows; High- ˊ Mid ˉ Low ˋ ... However, of these, only the mid-tone occurs on monosyllabic roots in isolation. ... The underlying system consists of glide tones which can apply either to single segments but form a system of suprasegmental patterns applied to polysyllabic words and compounds. ... Kman is a sesquisyllabic language of a type common in the SE Asian region. Structurally, many words consist of a presyllable or minor syllable plus root. However, as a highly tonal language, this presyllable bears an unpredictable tone.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Kman/Geman is described as a lexical tone language (three tone heights plus glide tonemes applied as word/compound-level suprasegmental patterns, floating tones over deleted presyllable vowels); the phonology chapters of every accessible description (Blench & Kri 2019 grammar and dictionary, Blench 2015, Das Gupta 1977) cover tone only and make no statement about word stress or accent.
new_statements.exceptions: None (no stress rule stated). Tone caveat from the source: tones in the grammar are marked as heard in context; the dictionary gives isolation tones; tones are 'highly mobile in compounds and sentence contexts'.
new_statements.domain_note: No stress domain stated. Word shape is sesquisyllabic (minor presyllable + root) with frequent vowel deletion in initial syllables, which implies root-final prominence but the source never frames it as stress.
new_statements.identity_note: gema1236 is a Glottolog 'Bookkeeping' languoid created for the retired ISO 639-3 code [gen] 'Geman Deng'. ISO 639-3 Change Request 2007-020 (downloaded, p.2) retired [gen] and merged it into [mxj] Miju Mishmi: 'the Ethnologue entries for India_Miju Mishmi_mxj and China_Geman Deng_gen are referring to the same language.. Kuman is an alternate name for Geman Deng and Kaman is an alternate name for Miju Mishmi.' The language is therefore Kman (= Kaman = Miju Mishmi = Chinese 格曼[僜]语), Glottolog miju1243, which is ALREADY in the catalog (classification tonal-OR-pitch accent from Blench & Kri 2019, verified by a second reader). Any gema1236 entry would duplicate miju1243 and should be merged/aliased, not counted as a distinct language. Blench & Kri describe the Indian side (Tezu / Lohit district, Arunachal Pradesh); the Chinese-side variety (Zayu county, Tibet) is the one described by Li Daqin 2002 and Sun Hongkai et al. 1980 under the name 格曼(僜)语. Note also that Sastry 1984 'Mishmi Grammar' (Glottolog files it under miju1243) actually describes the Digaru (Taraon) dialect (Introduction p.5: 'data collected.. in Tezu and Tafrogam from the Digaru dialect'; Miju data used only for cross-checking) -- i.e. Digaro-Mishmi, not Kman.
